headline: Tom Cruise checks on a woman lost in her phone

sources.title: The cure for doomscrolling? Why Tom Cruise stopped a woman mid-scroll (The Guardian)
Tom Cruise surprises woman doomscrolling at work, viral video wins hearts online (WION)
Tom Cruise Surprises Woman While She's "Doomscrolling" In Viral Video (iHeart)

chunks.text: Tom Cruise has [[gone viral]] for a small [[act of kindness]]. Security camera [[footage]] shared online in late September 2026 shows him walking past the open door of a [[break room]] at a workplace. Inside, a woman sat with her back to the door, her head bent low over her phone. Her [[body language]] {{gave off}} signs of [[distress]]. Cruise {{picked up on}} those signs and stopped. He stepped inside and tapped her shoulder to check on her.

verbs.correct: To show a sign or feeling
verbs.wrong: To copy a sign or feeling
verbs.why: Some people give off confidence the moment they walk in. Tired eyes often give off signs of stress. From behind, the woman's body language gave off signs of distress.
Kids pick up on small changes at home. Good teachers pick up on a nervous smile right away. Cruise picked up on the woman's posture and stopped.

chunks.text: It {{turned out}} nothing was wrong. The woman was only [[doomscrolling]], or reading negative posts online for a long time. When she saw who it was, she could only say, "Tom Cruise?" The tap on the shoulder made her {{snap out of}} it. The two shared a [[fist bump]], and he wished her a good night. Cruise {{came back}} for a photo after she had {{gotten over}} the [[shock]].

verbs.wrong: To be filmed by a fan's phone
verbs.why: It often turns out that the cheap option costs more. A quiet coworker often turns out to be very funny. It turned out that the woman was only doomscrolling.

verbs.correct: To suddenly stop a bad habit or mood
verbs.wrong: To feel very tired and sleepy
verbs.why: Most people snap out of a bad mood after a walk. Drivers snap out of a daydream when the light turns green. The tap on the shoulder made the woman snap out of her doomscrolling.

verbs.wrong: To call a guard for help
verbs.why: The repairman comes back the next day with the right part. Shoppers often come back for a forgotten bag. Cruise came back later so the woman could take a photo with him.

verbs.correct: To feel normal again after a shock
verbs.wrong: To leave a place in a hurry
verbs.why: Most people get over the shock of a big bill in a few days. Kids get over a scary movie quickly. The woman had gotten over the shock by the time Cruise came back.

chunks.text: The woman later posted the footage on TikTok. "He literally tapped me on my shoulder, and I don't remember what he said," she wrote. "I was in complete shock." The clip quickly {{took off}} and {{ended up}} on X and other [[platforms]]. Many viewers [[praised]] Cruise for stopping. One person on X called him "just a kind man." A Guardian writer joked that doomscrolling can make anyone look deeply upset from behind.

verbs.wrong: To be saved on a work computer
verbs.why: Songs often take off after a famous singer shares them. New apps sometimes take off during the summer. The woman's clip took off on TikTok.
Tourists often take the wrong bus and end up downtown. Letters with old addresses end up at a neighbor's house. The video ended up on X and other platforms.

chunks.text: Doomscrolling is not only a joke, though. Research has shown that it can increase [[anxiety]], [[depression]] and stress. It can also cause [[physical discomfort]]. The British government is {{looking into}} limits on apps that let people scroll without end. The video spread during a busy week for Cruise. His new film, Digger, is a [[dark comedy]] that {{came out}} in North America on October 2, 2026. It is his first movie in years that is not an action film.

verbs.why: Many companies look into a four-day work week. Some towns look into free buses for everyone. The British government is looking into limits on apps that let people scroll without end.

verbs.correct: To become available to the public
verbs.why: A new book in a popular series comes out every spring. Fans wait in line when a new game comes out. Digger came out in North America on October 2, 2026.

mainIdea.s: A security camera filmed Tom Cruise stopping to help a worker who looked upset over her phone. Nothing was wrong, and the clip spread widely just as his new film came out.
mainIdea.why: Cruise stopped to help the woman because her posture suggested distress. It turned out she was only doomscrolling, and the video took off in the week Digger came out.

mainIdea.s: The actor comforted a worker who was crying after reading terrible news on her phone. She later shared the security video, and many viewers praised the actor for being so caring.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the woman was not crying or truly upset. It turned out she was only doomscrolling, and her posture made Cruise think she was in distress.

mainIdea.s: The actor says he is taking a long break from social media to protect his health. He wants his fans to spend less time on their phones and more time with family and friends.
mainIdea.why: Cruise made no such announcement. He stopped to help a woman he thought was in distress, and she turned out to be doomscrolling.

tf.s: Cruise picked up on signs that a woman might be in distress.
tf.why: Her body language gave off signs of distress, so he stopped and tapped her on the shoulder.

tf.s: It turned out that the woman was having a medical emergency.
tf.why: Nothing was wrong with her. It turned out she was only doomscrolling on her phone.

tf.s: Cruise posed for a photo with the woman as soon as he tapped her shoulder.
tf.why: They shared a fist bump first. He came back after she had gotten over the shock, and they took the photo then.

tf.s: The clip of Cruise and the woman quickly took off online.
tf.why: Many viewers praised Cruise for stopping, and the clip ended up on X and other platforms.

tf.s: The British government has already banned apps that let people scroll without end.
tf.why: There is no ban yet. The government is only looking into limits on these apps.

tf.s: A tap on the shoulder from Cruise made the woman snap out of her doomscrolling.
tf.why: When she saw who it was, she could only say his name. The two shared a fist bump.

lines.text: Did you see the video of Tom Cruise in that break room?
A woman was sitting with her back to the door, [[glued to her phone]]. Cruise saw her from the hallway and stopped.
Her body language {{gave off}} signs of distress. He {{picked up on}} it and tapped her shoulder to see if she was OK.
Totally fine. It {{turned out}} she was just doomscrolling.
So a movie star appeared [[out of nowhere]] because she was reading bad news?
Basically. The tap made her {{snap out of}} it, and all she could say was "Tom Cruise?"
She was. He {{came back}} after she had {{gotten over}} the shock, and they took a photo together.
For sure. She posted the security footage, and it {{took off}}. It {{ended up}} all over X.
People love a story like that. A little kindness [[goes a long way]].
There's a serious side, though. The British government is {{looking into}} limits on apps that let you scroll forever.
Good. Doesn't Cruise have a new film, too?
Yes, Digger. It {{came out}} in North America on October 2.
Well, I think I'll spend less time on my phone tonight.

expressions.def: Used to say someone is looking at their phone and paying attention to nothing else
ex: He sat glued to his phone during the whole dinner.

expressions.def: Used to say something happens suddenly, with no warning
ex: A deer ran into the road out of nowhere.

expressions.def: So excited near a famous person that you cannot act normally
ex: My son was starstruck when he met his favorite player.

expressions.def: Used to say something made a person very happy that day
ex: Your kind note really made my day.
The free coffee made his day.

expressions.def: Used to say a small thing can have a big good effect
ex: A smile goes a long way with new customers.
Saying thank you goes a long way at work.
